newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica golds eye gloomy week under dismal bullion.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica golds eye gloomy week under dismal bullion.

text.p: South African gold stocks are set for a dreary week, cowering in the shadow of a fading bullion price, dealers and portfolio managers said on Friday.

Briefly fooling metal shares with a bounce at the start of the week, the gold price has since collapsed to the $344 level and dealers said it was likely to crumble to $342 soon, before plummeting to the key $330 an ounce support level.
After a short-lived rally, South African gold shares shed all gains and are now eyeing a week of further wasting.
"There is going to be continued weakness in gold shares," said James Scott, senior dealer at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak.
"Gold is under continued pressure. Technically it's looking to test shortly the $342 level, that's soft support there, and then major support at the $330 level," he said.

Dealers added that the stronger rand this week did not bode well for metal stocks, whose only protection against a failing dollar gold price was to boost export earnings through a weaker local currency.
At 1040 GMT the rand was bid at 4.5640 against the dollar. The rand began the year around the 4.70 level.
The outlook for industrial stocks, however, puzzled the market and commentators varied on next week's forecast.

"At this stage we're seeing a very, very strange market. The American market is rosy, bonds are rosy, the European markets are rosy, S&P futures are rosy...Everything is good except this (stock) market," said Greg Amoils, Irish & Co portfolio manager. Dealers and portfolio managers said that industrials had recently been under a great deal of pressure which could be linked to either futures trade or asset swaps.
"It could possibly be asset swap related. There is a very large seller of stocks in this market and of the large stocks too. The lead is coming from the futures market," Amoils said.
Others said that it appeared that futures were being sold heavily and were dragging stocks down slightly.
Some commentators, however, said that against this scenario of a manipulated market were reasonably good economic indicators which should ensure a firmer industrial market next week.
But others said that another large asset swap could be about to take place, which would weigh the market.

Another market worry was that Wall Street's record closes had held little sway over the Johannesburg Stock Exchange and new fears were arising of the extent of the negative impact on local stocks if the U.S. market dropped.

"The problem is that markets in general are at record highs. What happens if they come off, as they must. What are we going to do," Amoils said, adding that there was a strong possibility South African shares could turn down next week.
"Although Johannesburg offers serious value right now it will turn around and I am a little bit nervous. We could turn around somtime next week," he said.
Countering this, other commentators said that institutional fund flow was still big and increasing.
"Institutions will continue to come to the market, so we expect better weeks ahead," Scott said.
